title: ACT-PREP PhD and Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026: Apply for 25 Funded Research Opportunities in Africa
summary: Apply for 15 ACT-PREP PhD and 10 postdoctoral research fellowships in clinical trials and epidemic preparedness. Review funding, eligibility, research themes, documents, partner universities and September 2026 deadlines. Applications are open for 25 ACT-PREP research fellowships designed to strengthen Africa’s capacity in clinical trials, infectious-disease surveillance, epidemic preparedness and emergency response. The current call offers: 15 PhD research fellowships. 10 postdoctoral research fellowships. The opportunities are available to eligible nationals of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda. Applicants must propose research connected to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness and response while meeting the academic and institutional requirements of their selected fellowship category. The programme provides tuition support, monthly stipends, research funding, mentorship, specialized training, access to research sites and datasets, and professional networking opportunities. The precise package depends on whether the candidate applies under PhD Round 1, PhD Round 2 or the postdoctoral category. The official announcement from Makerere University was published on August 14, 2026. ACT-PREP Research Fellowships at a Glance Programme detail Information Programme ACT-PREP Available opportunities 15 PhD and 10 postdoctoral positions Main fields Clinical trials and epidemic preparedness and response research Funding programme HORIZON-JU-GH-EDCTP3 PhD funding period Up to three years Postdoctoral funding period Up to 12 months PhD Round 1 deadline September 15, 2026 PhD Round 2 deadline September 30, 2026 Postdoctoral deadline September 30, 2026 Eligible nationalities DRC, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda Application languages English or French Application method Submission by email Number of priority themes Seven Female applicants Strongly encouraged Application fee No application fee is stated What Is ACT-PREP? ACT-PREP is a multi-country research and capacity-strengthening initiative focused on improving Africa’s preparedness for infectious-disease outbreaks and other public-health emergencies. The project seeks to strengthen the continent’s ability to conduct timely, ethical and scientifically rigorous clinical research before and during disease outbreaks. It focuses on institutionalizing clinical-trial preparedness within national public-health systems instead of treating research as a separate activity that begins only after an emergency occurs. According to the official Global Health EDCTP3 project profile , ACT-PREP runs from June 1, 2026, to May 31, 2031. The wider project has been awarded approximately €12.75 million in Global Health EDCTP3 funding. This amount represents funding for the overall multi-year ACT-PREP project. It is not the individual amount payable to each fellow. The initiative aims to build clinical research and outbreak-response capacity through: PhD and postdoctoral research support. Short- and long-term professional training. Mentorship programmes. Research exchanges. Access to real-world datasets. Practical training at clinical-trial and surveillance sites. Training for clinical-trial monitors. Strengthening of ethics and regulatory-review systems. Improved surveillance and health-information systems. Laboratory and data-management upgrades. Standardized outbreak-research protocols. Community engagement. Institutional and regional research partnerships. The wider project intends to train more than 700 senior researchers in advanced methods, support 15 PhD students and 10 postdoctoral researchers, and train an additional 80 clinical-trial monitors. Why the ACT-PREP Programme Is Needed Africa continues to experience a substantial burden of infectious diseases and public-health emergencies. The official call reports that the African region recorded 2,234 acute public-health events between 2001 and 2022. Approximately 92% were infectious-disease events, while zoonotic outbreaks increased substantially during the period. Recent outbreaks have repeatedly revealed structural limitations, including: Fragmented disease-surveillance systems. Weak integration of human, animal and environmental health information. Delayed laboratory confirmation. Limited diagnostic infrastructure. Slow deployment of outbreak research. Inadequate readiness to launch clinical trials during emergencies. Limited research coordination across countries. Delays in ethics and regulatory review. Insufficient pharmacovigilance capacity. Weak integration of research into emergency-response systems. ACT-PREP seeks to address these gaps by strengthening research, surveillance, ethics, diagnostics, pharmacovigilance, regulation and policy across Africa’s emergency preparedness and response ecosystem. Diseases and Public-Health Areas Covered ACT-PREP has a broad infectious-disease and health-security mandate. Its wider programme focuses particularly on: HIV and AIDS. Malaria. Tuberculosis. Neglected tropical diseases. Emerging infectious diseases. Re-emerging infectious diseases. Epidemic-prone pathogens. Zoonotic diseases. Outbreak-related clinical research. Applicants should ensure that their proposed research is relevant to the programme’s mandate and to an EDCTP-priority disease or health-security challenge. Seven ACT-PREP Priority Research Themes Applicants must align their proposed work with at least one of the following research themes: 1. Clinical Trials and Trial Readiness This theme can include work on: Clinical-trial design and implementation. Trial-site preparedness. Rapid activation of trials during outbreaks. Clinical research quality systems. Participant recruitment and retention. Trial-monitoring approaches. Community engagement in clinical research. Standardized outbreak-trial protocols. Trial data quality and management. 2. Disease Surveillance, Modelling and Artificial Intelligence Relevant research may address: Early-warning systems. Disease forecasting. Epidemiological modelling. Digital surveillance. Artificial intelligence for outbreak detection. Integration of surveillance information. Analysis of routine health data. Predictive analytics. Data visualization for emergency response. Integration with health-information systems such as DHIS2. 3. Ethics and Regulatory Science This area may include: Ethics-review procedures during outbreaks. Regulatory preparedness. Rapid but responsible research review. Protection of research participants. Digital systems for ethics and regulatory authorities. Regulatory coordination across countries. Pharmacovigilance regulation. Ethical governance of emergency research. Research integrity. 4. Laboratory and Genomic Surveillance Possible topics include: Genomic sequencing. Pathogen detection. Diagnostic technologies. Laboratory quality systems. Molecular epidemiology. Laboratory-network strengthening. Data management for genomic surveillance. Rapid diagnostic confirmation. Laboratory preparedness for epidemics. 5. One Health This theme recognizes the connection between human, animal and environmental health. Research can explore: Zoonotic-disease surveillance. Human-animal transmission pathways. Environmental drivers of outbreaks. Integrated surveillance systems. Collaboration between medical, veterinary and environmental institutions. Community-level disease prevention. Cross-sector emergency preparedness. 6. Health-Systems Resilience Relevant work may examine: Health-system continuity during emergencies. Preparedness of healthcare facilities. Workforce readiness. Supply chains during outbreaks. Integration of research into routine public-health systems. Emergency governance. Community trust and engagement. Equitable access to emergency interventions. 7. Epidemic Preparedness and Response This broad area can cover: National and regional preparedness. Emergency-response systems. Outbreak investigation. Rapid research deployment. Policy responses. Public-health communication. Emergency coordination. Evaluation of preparedness plans. Lessons from previous epidemics. PhD Fellowships: Two Application Routes ACT-PREP has created two separate PhD application rounds. Applicants must select the correct route based on whether they are already enrolled in a doctoral programme. PhD Round 1: Currently Enrolled Doctoral Researchers PhD Round 1 is intended for applicants who are already enrolled in a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university. Applicants must already be conducting or developing doctoral research under one of the seven ACT-PREP priority themes. PhD Round 1 Eligibility Applicants should: Be nationals of an eligible ACT-PREP country. Hold a relevant master’s degree or equivalent qualification. Have an academic background in health, biomedical sciences, public health or a related discipline. Be currently enrolled in a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university. Propose research aligned with an ACT-PREP priority theme. Obtain formal endorsement from their home institution. Provide two suitable referees. Submit every required document before the closing date. Commit to research quality, integrity and timely completion. PhD Round 1 Duration Fellows are expected to complete their doctoral programme within three years. A justified no-cost extension may be considered under applicable university policies and approval procedures. Such an extension would not automatically provide additional fellowship funding. PhD Round 1 Financial and Academic Support The package may include: Partial or full tuition and university fees. A monthly stipend. A one-time research or clinical-trial grant. Mentorship from ACT-PREP specialists. Core training courses. Specialized courses connected to the research theme. Access to consortium trial sites. Access to relevant datasets. Participation in research and mentorship networks. Access to alumni opportunities. The call does not state the monetary value of the monthly stipend or one-time research grant. PhD Round 1 Deadline September 15, 2026 PhD Round 2: Applicants Seeking Doctoral Enrolment PhD Round 2 is intended for candidates who are not necessarily enrolled in a doctoral programme but are eligible and willing to register at an ACT-PREP partner university. These applicants must commit to completing their doctoral training within three years. PhD Round 2 Eligibility Applicants should: Be nationals of an ACT-PREP partner country. Hold a relevant master’s degree or equivalent. Have a suitable academic background in health, biomedical sciences, public health or a related field. Be eligible to register for a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university. Propose work under one of the seven priority themes. Secure institutional endorsement. Identify an appropriate host institution and mentor. Provide two referees. Commit to completing doctoral training within three years. Applicants affiliated with an ACT-PREP institution, including eligible junior researchers, will receive priority consideration. PhD Round 2 Support The fellowship may provide: Tuition and university fees. A monthly stipend. A one-time research or clinical-trial grant. Mentorship from ACT-PREP experts. Core and specialized training courses. Access to research sites and datasets. Professional networking. Alumni and mentorship opportunities. The fellowship can be supported for up to three years, subject to programme and institutional requirements. PhD Round 2 Deadline September 30, 2026 Postdoctoral Research Fellowships The ten postdoctoral positions are designed to help early-career African researchers develop independent research leadership in clinical trials and epidemic preparedness. Selected researchers will join ongoing ACT-PREP research activities while developing and leading their own research outputs. Their work must either: Integrate appropriate clinical-trial methodologies; or Address a substantive epidemic preparedness and response topic. Postdoctoral researchers will be expected to uphold high standards of research quality, ethics and integrity. Postdoctoral Eligibility Applicants must: Be nationals of an eligible ACT-PREP country. Hold a PhD in a relevant health, biomedical or related field. Have obtained the PhD within the past five years. Demonstrate a research record appropriate to their postdoctoral career stage. Propose research aligned with an ACT-PREP priority theme. Confirm an appropriate host institution. Obtain endorsement from the home or host institution. Identify a suitable mentor. Provide two referees. Demonstrate potential for research leadership and scientific independence. Submit a complete application before the deadline. Postdoctoral Support Selected postdoctoral researchers may receive: A mentored position at a consortium partner institution. A monthly stipend. Research support. Mobility support. Funding for up to 12 months. Training in scientific writing. Training in research leadership. Training in grant administration. Specialized methodological training. Exposure to modelling, bioinformatics and real-world evidence methods. Support to publish research. Support to present findings at conferences. Guidance on securing follow-on research funding. Mentorship from local and international experts. The call does not specify the stipend, research-support or mobility-support amounts. Postdoctoral Deadline September 30, 2026 Eligible ACT-PREP Countries Applicants must be nationals of one of the following seven countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo. Rwanda. Senegal. Somalia. South Sudan. Tanzania. Uganda. Citizenship or nationality is required. Residence in one of these countries without holding an eligible nationality may not satisfy the requirement. ACT-PREP Partner Universities The PhD opportunities are connected to the following universities: Makerere University , Uganda. Somali National University , Somalia. Université de Kinshasa , Democratic Republic of the Congo. Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences , Tanzania. University of Global Health Equity , Rwanda. Université Cheikh Anta Diop , Senegal. University of Juba , South Sudan. PhD Round 1 applicants must already be enrolled at a relevant ACT-PREP partner university. Round 2 applicants must be eligible to register at a partner university. Postdoctoral applicants must confirm an appropriate host institution and obtain the required institutional endorsement. Application Languages Applications may be prepared in: English; or French. French-language applications are accepted, particularly from applicants connected to francophone ACT-PREP institutions, including Université de Kinshasa and Université Cheikh Anta Diop. Applicants should use one language consistently and ensure that all documents are clear, professionally written and complete. Required Application Documents Applicants should submit a complete application package containing the following: 1. Completed Application Form Applicants must complete Document D from the official application package. The form requests: Full name. Sex or gender. Nationality. Date of birth. Email address. Telephone number. Current position. Current institution. Nominating or home institution. Academic qualifications. Proposed research title. Selected ACT-PREP research theme. Proposed host institution. Proposed mentor or mentors. Signed declaration. 2. Academic Documents Applicants should provide copies of relevant: Degrees. Academic certificates. Transcripts where required. Proof of current doctoral enrolment for Round 1. Evidence of eligibility for doctoral registration for Round 2. Proof of PhD completion date for postdoctoral applicants. 3. Updated Curriculum Vitae The CV should clearly present: Education. Research experience. Employment history. Research projects. Technical and analytical skills. Research methods. Conference participation. Professional affiliations. Awards or recognition. Relevant training. Publications. Postdoctoral applicants should include a complete or appropriately selected publication list. 4. Research Concept Note Applicants must prepare a research concept of approximately two to three pages. It should include: Working research title. Selected ACT-PREP priority theme. Background and rationale. Research problem. Objectives. Proposed methodology. Expected results or contributions. Relevance to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness. Alignment with an EDCTP-priority disease. Implementation work plan. Proposed host institution. Proposed mentor or supervisory arrangement. Expected contribution to African research capacity. The work plan must be realistic for the fellowship duration. PhD applicants should design work that can be completed within three years, while postdoctoral candidates should present a plan achievable within 12 months. 5. Motivation Letter The motivation letter should explain: Why the applicant is interested in ACT-PREP. How the opportunity relates to the applicant’s career. The applicant’s relevant academic and research experience. Why the selected research theme is important. How the applicant will contribute to the consortium. The applicant’s commitment to research quality and integrity. How the applicant intends to strengthen research and epidemic preparedness in Africa. The applicant’s intention to remain connected to and contribute to the region. 6. Institutional Endorsement Letter An institutional endorsement or nomination letter is mandatory for both PhD and postdoctoral applicants. It should be prepared on the nominating institution’s official letterhead and confirm: The candidate’s status as a staff member, registered researcher or person eligible to enrol. The institution’s formal support for the application. Alignment of the proposed work with institutional priorities. Willingness to host and support the fellow. Availability of mentorship. Support for enrolment where applicable. Permission to participate in ACT-PREP training and research activities. Institutional support throughout the fellowship period. 7. Two References Applicants must identify two referees. The application checklist also requires two reference letters. Referees should comment on: How long they have known the applicant. The capacity in which they know the applicant. The applicant’s research ability. Research independence. Suitability for the fellowship. Potential for research leadership. Likelihood of timely completion. Motivation. Integrity. Teamwork. The official guidance instructs referees to submit their recommendations directly to the recruitment email by the applicable deadline. Applicants should therefore contact referees early and confirm that their letters have been sent. How to Apply Applications must be submitted electronically by email. Primary Submission Address recruitment@act-prep.org Addresses to Copy actprep@musph.ac.ug noahzyah@gmail.com Applicants should attach all required documents and clearly identify whether they are applying for: PhD Round 1. PhD Round 2. Postdoctoral Fellowship. Although the call does not prescribe a mandatory email subject, candidates should use a clear subject that identifies the fellowship category and their full name. Applicants should use the forms and templates included in the official application package . Application Deadlines Fellowship route Deadline PhD Round 1 September 15, 2026 PhD Round 2 September 30, 2026 Postdoctoral Fellowship September 30, 2026 The announcement does not specify a closing time or time zone. Applicants should submit well before the relevant date and obtain confirmation that the application has been received. Selection Process Applications will undergo a competitive, multi-stage selection process. Stage 1: Application Screening The selection team will verify: Completeness. Eligible nationality. Required academic qualification. Programme enrolment or registration eligibility. Institutional endorsement. Presence of two referees. Research-theme alignment. Submission by the deadline. Incomplete or ineligible applications may not proceed. Stage 2: Scientific Evaluation Eligible applications will undergo scientific review. Reviewers will assess: Quality of the research concept. Scientific merit. Relevance. Feasibility. Alignment with ACT-PREP themes. Alignment with EDCTP priorities. Potential contribution to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness. Likely scientific or public-health impact. Suitability of the work plan. Stage 3: Interviews Shortlisted applicants will be invited to an interview to evaluate: Academic and research readiness. Understanding of the proposed research. Motivation. Communication. Suitability for the fellowship. Ability to complete the research within the available time. Potential for research leadership. Fit with the proposed host and mentor. Stage 4: Notification Successful candidates will receive formal notification following the selection process. title: Berenson Fellowship 2027–2028 at Harvard University’s I Tatti: $5,200 Monthly Funding for Renaissance Scholars in Florence, Italy
summary: The Berenson Fellowship at Harvard University’s Villa I Tatti – The Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies offers an exceptional residential research opportunity for scholars whose work explores the connections between Italy and the wider world during the Renaissance. Supported by The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund , the fellowship is designed to encourage research into “Italy in the World” by examining the transnational exchanges, encounters, dialogues, and cultural relationships between Italy and other regions during the Renaissance, broadly understood as the period from the 14th through the 17th century . The fellowship is particularly interested in research that moves beyond a narrowly European understanding of the Renaissance and examines Italy’s relationships with cultures and societies across regions such as Africa, the Mediterranean, Latin America, and Asia . Selected Fellows will be based in Florence, Italy , where they will have dedicated time for research, access to Harvard’s extensive scholarly resources at I Tatti, and opportunities to participate in the intellectual life of the Center. The fellowship provides USD 5,200 per month , in addition to a relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800 . Up to four Berenson Fellowships are awarded each year , making this a highly selective opportunity for established and emerging scholars working on original research related to the Renaissance and its global connections. What Is the Berenson Fellowship? The Berenson Fellowship is a residential research fellowship hosted by Villa I Tatti – The Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies in Florence. The fellowship takes its name from Bernard Berenson , an influential scholar and art historian associated with I Tatti. In his 1956 statement, “On the Future of I Tatti,” Berenson expressed a vision in which scholars would come from different parts of the world and develop a broad understanding of the Mediterranean and its surrounding regions. The Berenson Fellowship builds on this vision by encouraging scholarship that examines the Renaissance from a geographically expansive perspective. Rather than treating the Renaissance solely as a European phenomenon, the fellowship seeks to support research investigating the connections between Italy and other cultures and regions . These connections may include: Cultural exchanges between Italy and Africa. Italy’s historical relationships with Mediterranean societies. Connections between Italy and Asian cultures. Transnational relationships involving Latin America. Intellectual exchanges across geographical boundaries. Movement of ideas, artistic traditions, texts, technologies, and people. Cross-cultural interactions during the Renaissance and early modern period. The influence of non-European cultures on Italian Renaissance developments. Italy’s role within wider networks of the early modern world. The fellowship therefore offers an opportunity for scholars to develop research that places the Italian Renaissance within a broader international and intercultural context. Berenson Fellowship Research Theme: “Italy in the World” The central theme of the fellowship is “Italy in the World.” Applicants are expected to propose projects that address transnational dialogues between Italy and other cultures during the Renaissance. The Renaissance is interpreted broadly for purposes of this fellowship, covering approximately the 14th to 17th centuries . This broad chronological and geographical approach allows researchers to investigate subjects that cross conventional disciplinary and regional boundaries. A strong project should therefore demonstrate how Italy was connected to wider intellectual, cultural, artistic, political, scientific, or social networks. For example, research could examine: Italian artistic exchanges with other regions. Mediterranean intellectual networks. African-Italian cultural encounters. Italian relationships with Asian societies. The circulation of Renaissance texts across borders. Music and musical traditions moving between cultures. Scientific knowledge exchanged between Italy and other regions. Philosophical interactions between Italian and non-Italian thinkers. Architectural influences crossing geographical boundaries. Literary connections between Italian writers and writers from other cultures. Trade, travel, migration, and their influence on Renaissance culture. The movement of artistic techniques, manuscripts, objects, and ideas. Cross-cultural encounters involving the Mediterranean and its hinterlands. The key consideration is that the project should contribute to a broader understanding of the Renaissance as a connected and geographically expansive historical phenomenon . Academic Fields Supported by the Fellowship The Berenson Fellowship welcomes scholars working across the range of disciplines supported by I Tatti. Applicants may come from fields including: Architecture and the Arts Researchers can investigate architecture, painting, sculpture, visual culture, material culture, artistic exchange, and related areas. Projects may explore how artistic ideas, styles, techniques, or objects moved between Italy and other parts of the world. History Historical research may examine political, social, cultural, economic, diplomatic, or intellectual relationships between Italy and other regions during the Renaissance. Philosophy Philosophical projects may explore intellectual exchanges, circulation of ideas, philosophical traditions, and relationships between Italian thinkers and intellectual traditions elsewhere. Literature Researchers may examine texts, literary movements, translation, cultural exchange, multilingual literary networks, and relationships between Italian and non-Italian literary traditions. Music Music scholars can investigate musical exchange, performance traditions, composers, instruments, musical theory, and the movement of music across geographical and cultural boundaries. History of Science Projects may investigate scientific knowledge, technologies, discoveries, instruments, scholarly networks, and intellectual exchanges linking Italy with other parts of the world. Applicants should ensure that their proposed project clearly fits within the intellectual scope of I Tatti while addressing the fellowship s emphasis on transnational connections. Why the Berenson Fellowship Is a Valuable Research Opportunity The fellowship is designed to provide scholars with something that is increasingly difficult to obtain: extended, uninterrupted time to focus primarily on research . I Tatti emphasizes a combination of substantial scholarly resources and relatively few obligations. Fellows can devote their time to developing their research project rather than balancing it with extensive teaching or administrative responsibilities. The fellowship provides: A residential research appointment in Florence. A grant of USD 5,200 per month . A relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800 . Access to the scholarly resources of Harvard s I Tatti Center. Access to the Biblioteca Berenson. A dedicated desk or carrel in the library. Opportunities to participate in the intellectual community at I Tatti. Participation in selected activities organized at the Center. Opportunities to attend conferences, lectures, and concerts. Interaction with scholars from different countries and academic disciplines. A research environment designed to minimize interruptions and obligations. These resources can be particularly valuable for scholars preparing a major scholarly publication, completing an extensive research project, or developing research that requires access to specialized materials available in Florence. Fellowship Duration The Berenson Fellowship is a residential fellowship lasting either four or six months . Applicants are asked to indicate their preferred fellowship period: Fall: September through December. Winter-Spring: January through June. The exact fellowship arrangement will depend on the appointment offered. Because the fellowship is residential, Fellows are expected to live in the Florence area and spend at least three days per week at I Tatti . This requirement reflects the Center s goal of creating an active scholarly community in which Fellows interact with other researchers and participate in the intellectual life of the institution. Financial Support and Fellowship Grant One of the major attractions of the Berenson Fellowship is its substantial financial support. Selected Fellows receive: Monthly Grant The fellowship provides a grant of: USD 5,200 per month This provides substantial financial support during the residential research period. Relocation Support In addition to the monthly grant, Fellows can receive a one-time relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800 . The supplement is intended to assist with expenses associated with relocating to Florence for the fellowship. Housing Because the fellowship is residential, Fellows must live in the Florence area. When possible, I Tatti will set aside an apartment for the Fellow s use. The apartment is provided rent free , although the Fellow is responsible for utility charges. If an I Tatti apartment is not available, the Center will provide a housing subsidy to help offset rental expenses. This housing arrangement can significantly reduce the cost of relocating to Florence for the fellowship period. Access to Harvard s Scholarly Resources Berenson Fellows enjoy the privileges available to Fellows at I Tatti. One of the most important resources is the Biblioteca Berenson , which Fellows can use seven days a week . This access is particularly important for scholars whose research requires specialized Renaissance materials and scholarly resources. Fellows also have their own desk or carrel in the Library . However, Term Fellows do not receive a separate private office or study. The research environment is therefore centered around the library and broader scholarly community of I Tatti. Participation in the I Tatti Intellectual Community Although Fellows receive substantial freedom to focus on their research, the fellowship is not intended to be an isolated research experience. Selected activities at I Tatti are reserved for Fellows, and Fellows are expected to become part of the wider scholarly community. They are expected to participate in activities such as: Conferences. Academic lectures. Concerts. Scholarly gatherings. Other intellectual activities organized by I Tatti. This community-oriented approach allows researchers to exchange ideas with scholars working across different disciplines and geographical areas. For applicants interested in building international academic networks, this aspect of the fellowship can be particularly valuable. Berenson Fellowship Eligibility Requirements Applicants must satisfy several important eligibility requirements. PhD Requirement At the time of application, candidates must already hold a PhD . Applicants will be required to upload a scan of their PhD certificate as part of the application process. This means the fellowship is not intended for doctoral students who are still completing their first PhD. Applicants Cannot Be Pursuing a Second PhD Candidates may not be working on a second PhD at the time of application . This requirement should be carefully considered by applicants who have completed one doctoral degree but are enrolled in another doctoral programme. Research Project Requirement Applicants must apply with a specific research project. The proposed project should align with the Berenson Fellowship s central focus on Italy in the World and the transnational relationships between Italy and other cultures during the Renaissance. The proposed research can form part of a larger scholarly project. However, applicants must be able to demonstrate that the specific project presented in the application is sufficiently developed and appropriate for the fellowship period. Full-Time Research Commitment Successful Fellows are expected to work solely on the project for which they applied . They are not permitted to simultaneously work on editing other book or article projects. This is an important condition because the fellowship is designed to provide uninterrupted time for a particular research project. Applicants should therefore select a project that can benefit substantially from four or six months of concentrated research. English and Italian Language Requirements Applicants must be: Conversant in English , and Familiar with Italian . The language requirement is important because the fellowship is based at an Italian Renaissance research center in Florence and involves engagement with Italian scholarly resources and the wider academic community. Research Must Be Feasible in Florence Applicants must demonstrate that it is possible to conduct most of their research in Florence . This does not necessarily mean that every source required for the project must be located in Florence. Rather, the proposed research should be sufficiently connected to the resources available in Florence to justify a residential appointment at I Tatti. Applicants should therefore carefully consider the research materials, archives, libraries, collections, and scholarly resources they will need during the fellowship. Priority for Early- and Mid-Career Scholars The fellowship gives priority to early- and mid-career scholars . This does not mean that senior scholars are necessarily excluded. Rather, the selection process gives particular consideration to applicants at earlier and middle stages of their academic careers. Candidates should therefore explain clearly how the fellowship would contribute to the development and advancement of their research. Global Eligibility: Scholars From All Nations Can Apply The Berenson Fellowship welcomes applications from scholars from all nations . There is no stated restriction limiting applications to a particular country, nationality, continent, or racial group. The fellowship specifically gives special consideration to candidates who do not have regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy . This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to scholars based outside Italy who would significantly benefit from spending an extended research period at I Tatti. Who Can Apply? In general, the opportunity is aimed at: Scholars who already hold a PhD. Researchers working in relevant Renaissance and early modern fields. Early-career scholars. Mid-career scholars. Scholars researching transnational relationships involving Italy. Researchers working in architecture and the arts. Historians. Philosophers. Literature scholars. Music scholars. Historians of science. Scholars whose projects can be substantially researched in Florence. Researchers conversant in English and familiar with Italian. Scholars from any country or nationality. The fellowship is therefore international in scope , and scholars from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, Oceania, the Middle East, and other regions may apply, provided they meet the academic and research requirements. Who Is Not Eligible? Potential applicants should take note of several restrictions. You may not qualify if: You do not yet have a PhD at the time of application. You are currently working toward a second PhD. Your proposed project cannot be substantially researched in Florence. You are unable to work in English and do not have familiarity with Italian. You intend to use the fellowship period to work simultaneously on unrelated books or articles. You plan to take on teaching or other professional obligations during the fellowship. You have previously held a Term Fellowship at I Tatti, except if you previously held a Graduate Fellowship. You have already used the fellowship opportunity in a way that conflicts with the Term Fellowship s one-time restriction. Applicants should carefully review the official application requirements before submitting their application. Previous I Tatti Appointments and One-Time Fellowship Rule Term Fellowships at I Tatti can be held only once . They also cannot be deferred . The fellowship is intended for scholars who have not previously held appointments at I Tatti , with the exception of Graduate Fellows. This means previous affiliation with I Tatti is an important factor to consider before applying. Restrictions During the Fellowship The residential fellowship comes with several obligations and restrictions. No Teaching Positions Fellows may not take on other obligations such as teaching positions , including part-time teaching, during any part of the fellowship period. Applicants who currently teach should therefore consider whether they can fully comply with this requirement. No Simultaneous Fellowship or Award The Berenson Fellowship may not be held concurrently with another fellowship or award . Applicants who receive external funding should carefully consider whether it can be held alongside the I Tatti fellowship. Outside Grants and Salary If an applicant receives a partial salary or outside grant, this information must be disclosed either: In the application, or In subsequent correspondence with the Director. Permission must also be received where required. Applicants should therefore be transparent about other sources of financial support. Visa and Health Insurance Responsibilities International Fellows are responsible for handling their own immigration and health-related arrangements. The Fellow is responsible for obtaining: A visa, where required. A permesso di soggiorno where applicable. Health coverage. Appropriate documentation for accompanying family members, where relevant. Applicants must determine whether they require a visa and, if one is necessary, obtain it before travelling . Prospective international applicants should therefore begin investigating Italian immigration requirements well before the fellowship start date. Application Process for the Berenson Fellowship Applications are submitted electronically . Applicants can prepare their application in either: English , or Italian . Candidates should ensure that all required application materials are completed and submitted through the designated online application system. The application should present a compelling research project and demonstrate the applicant s scholarly ability and potential contribution to I Tatti s intellectual community. What Makes a Strong Application? Although selection is competitive, several elements are explicitly important in the evaluation process. The selection committee pays particular attention to: The strength of the proposed project The potential of the project to produce original results The candidate s curriculum vitae The candidate s ability to contribute collegially to I Tatti s intellectual life Applicants should therefore avoid treating the application as simply a funding request. Instead, the application should demonstrate: A clearly defined research question. A strong understanding of existing scholarship. A convincing explanation of the project s originality. A realistic research plan. A strong connection to the “Italy in the World” theme. A clear reason why Florence and I Tatti are important for the research. Evidence of the applicant s scholarly achievements. The potential significance of the expected results. Letters of Recommendation Applicants must arrange for two scholars who know their work well to submit recommendations online. The recommendation letters may be written in: English, or Italian. The referees must submit their recommendations electronically by: November 21, 2026 Applicants are strongly encouraged to register their referees early through the reference section of the application system. Once registered, referees will receive an email explaining how to access the system and submit their recommendations. Applicants are responsible for informing their referees about: The nature of the proposed research project. The fellowship being applied for. The application deadline. The separate recommendation deadline. Giving referees adequate notice can help ensure that recommendations are submitted on time. Berenson Fellowship Deadlines There are two important dates applicants should remember. Main Application Deadline November 16, 2026 Applications must be submitted electronically by midnight Cambridge, Massachusetts time on November 16, 2026 . Recommendation Letter Deadline November 21, 2026 The two required recommendation letters must be submitted online by November 21, 2026 . Because the recommendation deadline comes after the main application deadline, applicants should not wait until the last minute to register their referees. Important Application Restriction Scholars may apply for only one type of I Tatti Fellowship per academic year . Applicants considering multiple I Tatti fellowship categories should therefore carefully determine which fellowship best matches their research and career circumstances before submitting an application. How to Prepare a Competitive Application Applicants interested in the Berenson Fellowship should approach the application strategically. 1. Develop a Clearly Defined Research Project Your project should have a clear research question and demonstrate why the subject matters. Avoid presenting a project that is too broad to complete meaningful work on during a four- or six-month residential fellowship. 2. Demonstrate the Transnational Dimension Because the fellowship focuses on “Italy in the World,” applicants should make the international or cross-cultural dimension of their research clear. Explain how the project examines relationships between Italy and another culture, region, society, intellectual tradition, or geographical area. 3. Explain Why Florence Matters A strong application should establish why conducting research at I Tatti and in Florence is important. Applicants should identify the resources, collections, scholarly environment, or research networks that make Florence particularly valuable for the project. 4. Emphasize Originality The selection committee specifically considers the potential of the proposed project to produce original results . Applicants should clearly explain what their research contributes that existing scholarship does not adequately address. 5. Present a Strong CV The curriculum vitae is an important component of the evaluation. Applicants should clearly present relevant: Academic qualifications. Publications. Research experience. Previous scholarly achievements. Fellowships and awards. Relevant academic positions. Conference participation. Other evidence of research ability. 6. Choose Appropriate Referees The two recommenders should know the applicant s scholarly work well enough to provide meaningful assessments. Applicants should give referees sufficient information about the proposed project so that their recommendations can address the candidate s research ability and potential. APPLY HERE Why Scholars From Outside Italy May Find This Fellowship Particularly Valuable The fellowship explicitly gives special consideration to candidates without regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy . This can be particularly significant for scholars based in countries where access to Italian Renaissance collections, archives, libraries, and specialized academic networks is limited. For researchers from Africa, Asia, Latin America, and other regions, the fellowship may provide an opportunity to access resources and develop scholarly relationships that would otherwise be difficult to obtain. The international character of the fellowship also fits the broader goal of encouraging geographically expansive approaches to Renaissance studies. Visit HERE to learn more about the Berenson Fellowship 2027–2028 at Harvard University’s I Tatti. Residential Nature of the Fellowship The Berenson Fellowship is not a remote fellowship. Successful Fellows must live in the Florence area and spend at least three days per week at I Tatti . Applicants should therefore be prepared for an extended period of residence in Italy. The residential requirement is central to the fellowship because I Tatti seeks to foster direct scholarly interaction among researchers. Applicants should consider accommodation, visa requirements, health coverage, travel, and other relocation arrangements when planning their application. The Broader Academic Value of the Fellowship Beyond the financial grant, the Berenson Fellowship can offer significant professional and intellectual value. Researchers have the opportunity to work in an environment specifically dedicated to Italian Renaissance studies while engaging with scholars from different academic backgrounds. The fellowship can support: Concentrated research. Development of original scholarship. Access to specialized library resources. International academic networking. Interdisciplinary collaboration. Exposure to different approaches to Renaissance studies. Development of manuscripts and other scholarly outputs. Deeper engagement with Italian research resources. Participation in an international scholarly community. For scholars whose projects require sustained concentration and access to specialized resources, this environment can be particularly valuable. title: MATS Residency Winter 2027: Fully Funded AI Safety Research Opportunity for Talented Researchers Worldwide
summary: The MATS Residency Winter 2027 is inviting talented individuals from around the world to apply for its upcoming intake, offering an opportunity to pursue ambitious research and safety-relevant projects focused on reducing catastrophic risks from advanced artificial intelligence. The Residency is designed for people who can demonstrate strong research ability and the potential to produce meaningful work in AI safety. Importantly, applicants are not required to have a PhD, a formal “researcher” job title, an extensive publication record, or previous AI safety experience . The Winter 2027 application window runs from 25 August to 31 October 2026 , giving prospective applicants several weeks to prepare and submit their applications. MATS Residency Winter 2027 The MATS Residency is intended to support individuals working on important questions surrounding AI alignment, AI safety, AI governance, evaluations, assurance and advanced AI systems . Rather than relying primarily on conventional academic credentials, the program evaluates the quality, seriousness and potential impact of an applicant’s work . This makes the Residency particularly relevant to talented researchers, technical professionals, policy experts, entrepreneurs and individuals transitioning into AI safety who can demonstrate that they have the ability to tackle difficult, open-ended problems. The program is also internationally accessible. Applicants can express a preference for one of three office locations — London, Berkeley or Washington, DC — and the Residency provides visa support for participants who need to relocate internationally. Apply for the MATS Residency Winter 2027 Opportunity Category Category: Fellowship / Research Residency The MATS Residency is a structured research program that supports participants in developing AI safety research, safety-relevant projects or incubation initiatives. MATS Residency Winter 2027 Deadline The application window for the Winter 2027 intake is: Opening date: 25 August 2026 Application deadline: 31 October 2026 Deadline timezone: Anywhere on Earth (AoE) Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day because the application requires several components, including references, a work sample and written responses. The next application window after the Winter 2027 intake is scheduled to open in March 2027 . When Will Applicants Hear Back? Applications are reviewed by the MATS Residency team, with input from program advisors where appropriate. The expected selection timeline is: Applications close: 31 October 2026. Application review: Applications are assessed by the Residency team. Application outcome: Applicants are expected to hear about the outcome by the end of November 2026. Interviews or paid work tests: Shortlisted applicants may be invited to an interview or paid work test during the first week of December 2026, depending on their track and research area. Final selection: Selected Residents are expected to be informed by the end of 2026. Residency start: Successful applicants are expected to begin in early 2027. Information about interviews and panel members will be provided to shortlisted applicants beforehand. Who Should Apply for the MATS Residency? One of the most important features of the MATS Residency is its approach to evaluating applicants. The program emphasizes what an applicant can do and the quality of their work , rather than simply looking at conventional credentials. You do not necessarily need: A PhD. A master s degree in AI safety. A job title containing the word “researcher.” A long list of academic publications. Previous professional experience specifically in AI safety. A conventional academic research career. The program is interested in talented individuals who can demonstrate the ability to produce outstanding AI safety research or safety-relevant work . This can include people whose strongest work is: Confidential. Unpublished. Conducted outside academia. Completed as part of an industry team. Based on technical or policy work. Demonstrated through projects rather than traditional publications. If an applicant is uncertain about whether their background qualifies, MATS encourages them to apply or contact the Residency team before submitting an application. What Research Does MATS Want to Support? Applicants are expected to submit a brief plan describing what they would like to accomplish during the Residency. Depending on the chosen track, this may take the form of: A research plan. A plan for safety-relevant work. A project plan. A plan to build or test an idea. A business or organizational plan for an incubation project. The proposed work should explain its theory of change — in other words, how the proposed research or project could ultimately contribute to improving AI safety and reducing catastrophic risks associated with advanced AI. 1. Impact MATS places significant emphasis on potentially high-impact work. The Residency is particularly interested in ambitious, longer-term projects that may not fit neatly within conventional academic or industry structures. Applicants should demonstrate why their proposed work could make a meaningful contribution to reducing catastrophic AI risk. 2. Depth The program is interested in foundational questions that may require substantial time and sustained investigation. Applicants should therefore think beyond projects that can be completed within a few weeks and instead consider research questions that could generate important insights over a longer period. Priority AI Safety Research Areas Although applicants are not restricted to a predetermined list of topics, MATS identifies several areas where it is particularly interested in supporting research. Safe Automation of Alignment Research One area of interest involves determining how AI systems can be used to accelerate alignment research while preserving meaningful human oversight. As AI systems become increasingly capable, researchers face an important challenge: how can AI-assisted research remain checkable, reliable and subject to appropriate oversight ? Research in this area may explore methods for ensuring that AI systems assisting with alignment research do not make the research process impossible for humans to adequately evaluate. Safety Cases, Evaluations, AI Strategy and AI Assurance MATS is also interested in work involving: AI safety cases. AI evaluations. AI strategy. AI assurance. Technical AI governance. These areas focus on building stronger evidence, methodologies and frameworks that can help organizations and policymakers make informed decisions about advanced AI. Research may contribute to ways of demonstrating that advanced AI systems meet particular safety requirements or establishing processes for evaluating their risks. Agentic and Multi-Agent AI Safety Another priority area concerns agentic and multi-agent AI systems . As AI systems become capable of acting more autonomously and interacting with other AI agents, new safety and alignment challenges can emerge. Research in this area may examine how autonomous systems should be designed, evaluated, monitored and aligned when they can independently pursue goals or interact with other systems. Applicants Are Not Limited to the Priority Areas The priority areas listed by MATS are intended to provide transparency about the research directions the program is particularly interested in supporting. They are not intended to prevent applicants from proposing other important AI alignment or AI safety research . Applicants should propose the work they genuinely believe is important and explain: What problem they are trying to solve. Why the problem matters. What they intend to investigate. How their proposed work could contribute to AI safety. What evidence would demonstrate progress. How the work could ultimately reduce catastrophic risks from AI. A strong theory of change can therefore be an important component of a competitive application. MATS Residency Office Locations Applicants can indicate a preferred office location when applying. The three locations are: London Berkeley Washington, DC The Residency follows a hybrid model . Residents are expected to spend at least one-third of their Residency working in person from the program s offices. There is no requirement to remain permanently assigned to one particular office. Residents may spend their in-person time at different MATS offices and can move between locations during the program. Applicants should therefore select the location that provides the strongest proximity to: Relevant AI research laboratories. Potential collaborators. Researchers. Technical communities. Policy communities. Other resources relevant to their proposed research. If multiple locations would be equally suitable, applicants can indicate this in their application. International Applicants The MATS Residency is open to applicants internationally . This is particularly important for researchers and professionals based outside the United States and United Kingdom. For successful applicants who need to relocate internationally, MATS states that it provides visa support . International applicants should nevertheless carefully consider their work-authorization circumstances and provide the required information in the application. MATS Residency Application Requirements Applicants must submit several components through the online application system. Preparation is therefore important, particularly for applicants who need to contact referees or prepare a representative research sample. 1. Short Profile and Eligibility Section Applicants begin by providing basic information for application processing and logistics. This section includes information such as: Contact details. Current affiliation. CV. Preferred office. Availability for the intake. Work-authorization status. Highest degree. Previous MATS involvement. The CV must be no longer than two pages . According to MATS, this section is primarily used for routing and logistical purposes rather than being the central component of the assessment. 2. Track Choice Applicants must select the MATS track that best fits their circumstances and proposed work. They are also asked to provide a brief explanation of approximately two to three sentences explaining why the selected track is appropriate. The track-selection explanation can help reviewers determine whether an applicant may be better suited to another pathway. 3. References Applicants must provide two references who can directly speak to the quality of their work. This is especially relevant for applicants whose strongest work is not publicly available. For example, if an applicant has worked on confidential research or contributed to a larger team, their referee may be able to verify the applicant s contribution. Some tracks have additional requirements concerning referees, so applicants should carefully review the requirements for their chosen track. 4. Representative Work Sample Applicants must submit one work sample that best demonstrates their strongest or most relevant work. Possible examples include: Academic papers. Research reports. Technical reports. Software repositories. Evaluations. Policy analyses. Other substantial research outputs. The strongest submission is not necessarily the most prestigious document. Applicants should select the work that best demonstrates their ability to conduct rigorous, valuable and independent work. 5. Written Responses Applicants must complete: Two short written responses. A brief counterfactual question concerning what they would do if they were not offered a place in the Residency. Applicants should use these responses to demonstrate their reasoning, motivation and ability to think clearly about their proposed work and future trajectory. MATS Residency Tracks The Winter 2027 Residency includes several tracks, each intended for different applicant profiles and career stages. Bridge Track The Bridge track is particularly relevant to applicants who may be entering AI safety from another field or who need additional time and support to develop their research portfolio. Applicants for Bridge must provide a research plan explaining: What they intend to work on. Why the research matters. How it could contribute to AI safety. Their theory of change. Why Bridge? Applicants should explain why the Residency is particularly valuable at their current stage. This could involve: Transitioning into AI safety. Developing a research direction. Strengthening an existing body of work. Getting dedicated research time. Addressing hiring constraints. Addressing visa or timing constraints. Applicants should also explain where they hope to go after the Residency and how participation would help them reach that next stage. Research Experience and Future Contribution Applicants should explain how their previous experience prepares them to contribute to AI safety research. For people transitioning from another field, this is an opportunity to highlight transferable: Research methods. Technical skills. Analytical abilities. Policy expertise. Domain knowledge. Unique perspectives. Applicants who already have AI safety experience should explain how additional time and support would allow them to deepen their research and prepare for their next opportunity. Anchor Track The Anchor track is designed for applicants for whom a longer-term research pathway is the appropriate next step. Applicants must submit a research plan and provide two referees who have directly supervised or evaluated their work. Suitable referees may include: Research supervisors. Collaborators. Senior colleagues. Other people with direct knowledge of the applicant s work. Why Anchor? Applicants should explain why a two-year staff researcher pathway is the appropriate next step for them. They should distinguish this pathway from alternatives such as: A PhD. A postdoctoral position. Another research role. Other professional opportunities. Evidence of Independent Work Applicants must demonstrate that they can take ownership of an open-ended problem and make meaningful progress. Evidence may include: Independent research. A thesis. Industry research. Technical projects. Policy work. Other comparable experience. Importantly, applicants do not need peer-reviewed publications or previous AI safety experience to demonstrate this capability. Incubation Track The Incubation track is intended for applicants seeking to develop a research agenda, research program or organization. Instead of submitting a conventional research plan, applicants provide a project plan explaining the direction they intend to develop and its theory of change. Incubation Rationale Applicants should explain: What is novel about their proposed direction. Why the idea requires dedicated time and support. Why MATS Incubation is an appropriate environment. What they hope to develop during the Residency. 90-Day Plan Applicants must outline what they intend to test or accomplish during their first 90 days . A strong plan should also identify what evidence would cause the applicant to: Revise the project. Pause the project. Stop the project altogether. This demonstrates that the applicant is prepared to learn from evidence rather than simply pursuing a predetermined idea. Governance and Publication Plan Where relevant, applicants should discuss: Governance. Publication strategy. Access to research outputs. Information hazards. Dual-use risks. This is particularly important for projects involving potentially sensitive AI safety research or technologies that could have both beneficial and harmful applications. Team and Resources Applicants should identify the expertise and resources required to execute their project. For projects involving the creation of an organization, applicants should also identify: Roles that still need to be filled. Skills required from future team members. How they would recruit suitable people. Use of AI Tools in the Application MATS allows applicants to use AI tools while preparing their applications. However, applicants are expected to be transparent about their use of AI. Applicants should: Briefly disclose whether they used AI tools. Explain how they used them. Confirm that they agree to the applicable AI-use policy. Ensure that the application reflects their own reasoning and judgment. MATS states that disclosed AI use is not, by itself, a reason for rejection . The important consideration is whether the application genuinely represents the applicant s own thinking and work. This can be particularly useful for applicants whose first language is not English. They may use AI tools to improve the clarity of their writing while retaining responsibility for the substance and reasoning of the application. Tips for Preparing a Strong MATS Residency Application Because the Residency emphasizes the quality of work rather than conventional credentials, applicants should focus on demonstrating ability, judgment and potential impact . 1. Develop a Clear Research Idea Avoid submitting a vague statement about wanting to “work in AI safety.” Instead, identify a specific problem and explain: What the problem is. Why it matters. What you intend to investigate. What existing approaches fail to address. What your proposed approach adds. What results would change your mind. 2. Focus on the Theory of Change Your application should make a clear connection between your research and improved AI safety. Explain how your research could move from: Research question → findings → practical application → improved safety → reduced catastrophic AI risk. 3. Select Your Strongest Work Sample Choose the work that best demonstrates your actual capabilities. A technically sophisticated project, rigorous analysis or strong independent research output may be more useful than simply submitting something because it has a prestigious affiliation. 4. Choose References Carefully Select people who can provide specific evidence about your abilities. A referee who has directly observed your research, technical work or analytical skills can potentially provide a much stronger assessment than someone who only knows you superficially. 5. Keep the CV Focused Because the CV is limited to two pages , applicants should prioritize: Relevant research. Significant projects. Technical or analytical achievements. Publications or substantial outputs. Relevant professional experience. Evidence of independent work. 6. Demonstrate Intellectual Independence The Residency is interested in people who can tackle difficult, open-ended problems. Where possible, show examples of situations in which you: Identified an important problem. Developed your own approach. Worked through uncertainty. Produced a substantive result. Changed your view based on evidence. 7. Do Not Overemphasize Credentials A lack of a PhD or previous AI safety job should not automatically discourage an applicant. Instead, use the application to demonstrate what you can actually contribute. 8. Contact MATS if You Are Unsure Applicants who are uncertain about: Their eligibility. The most appropriate track. The appropriate office. The suitability of their research idea. can contact the MATS Residency team before applying. The official contact is residency@matsprogram.org . Why the MATS Residency Winter 2027 Is Worth Considering The program offers an opportunity for talented individuals to dedicate substantial time to difficult AI safety questions while engaging with an international research community. Potential advantages include: Developing advanced AI safety research experience. Working on ambitious and potentially high-impact research questions. Connecting with researchers and collaborators. Accessing an established AI safety research environment. Developing a stronger research portfolio. Transitioning from another field into AI safety. Pursuing longer-term research through the Anchor pathway. Developing a new research project or organization through Incubation. Accessing international offices in London, Berkeley and Washington, DC. Receiving visa support where international relocation is required. The precise experience will depend on the applicant s selected track, research direction and individual circumstances. How to Apply for the MATS Residency Winter 2027 Interested applicants should begin by reviewing the official Residency information and application requirements. The application can be submitted online through the official MATS application system. MATS Residency Winter 2027 Application Applicants should make sure they have sufficient time to prepare their research or project plan, identify appropriate referees, select a representative work sample and complete the written responses. MATS does not restrict the Residency to people with a particular race, nationality or continent. The program explicitly states that the Residency is open internationally , meaning applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania and other regions worldwide may apply, subject to the program s application and logistical requirements. title: UN Political Integrity Traineeship 2026 in Brussels: Paid 6-Month EU Policy and Anti-Corruption Opportunity at Transparency International EU
summary: The Transparency International EU Political Integrity Traineeship 2026 offers an opportunity for an early-career professional to gain practical experience in EU policy, political integrity, anti-corruption research, policy analysis, communications and project support while working with Transparency International EU in Brussels, Belgium. TI EU is part of the wider Transparency International movement , working closely with Transparency International national chapters in more than 100 countries around the world and with the Transparency International Secretariat based in Berlin. The organisation coordinates Transparency International s advocacy towards the European Union institutions . Its mission is focused on: Preventing corruption. Promoting integrity. Promoting transparency. Promoting accountability in EU institutions. Influencing EU policies and legislation. Supporting efforts to fight corruption at national level. Promoting equality and access to justice for citizens. The EU Political Integrity Traineeship therefore offers an opportunity to work within an organisation whose activities connect European-level policymaking with broader efforts to strengthen integrity, transparency and accountability. The successful trainee will work as an EU Policy Trainee and assist the office with its work on EU political integrity. A major component of the role will involve responding to on-demand policy and research requests from senior team members . The position provides exposure to a range of activities rather than concentrating on a single area. The trainee may contribute to policy research, anti-corruption monitoring, investigative analysis, events, project implementation, reporting, communications and administrative support. This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to graduates and early-career professionals interested in: European Union affairs EU institutions Public policy Political science International relations Law Economics European studies Anti-corruption Transparency and accountability Governance Public-sector integrity Policy research Advocacy Communications Key Details at a Glance Opportunity Details Organisation Transparency International EU Position EU Policy Trainee Opportunity type Traineeship Start date 5 October 2026 Duration 6 months Location Brussels, Belgium Work arrangement Hybrid: teleworking and office-based work Working hours 38 hours per week Contract Convention d’Immersion Professionnelle under Belgian law Allowance EUR 1,200 gross per month Application language English Application deadline 6 September 2026, 23:59 Brussels time Interview period Week of 14 September 2026 Work experience requirement Early-career applicants; no more than 5+ years of relevant experience Degree requirement University degree or equivalent experience in a relevant field Work eligibility Legal right to reside and work in Belgium What Will the Trainee Do? This can include providing support for: Project management Project reporting General project activities The role therefore provides exposure to the operational side of policy and advocacy work in addition to research. 5. Track Activities, Impact and Reporting The trainee will assist with tracking activities and impact and supporting reporting to external actors. This responsibility may involve helping the organisation document progress and communicate results to external stakeholders. title: MOVE Fund 2026: Apply for Two-Year Grants of $40,000–$150,000 for Sport and Youth Development Coalitions
summary: The MOVE Fund 2026 is inviting eligible coalitions and collectives working at the intersection of sport, play, youth development, equity, and community systems to participate in its 2026 funding opportunity. The fund is designed to support collaborative groups seeking to strengthen sport-based youth development, advocate for increased investment in sport and play, and help create local sports systems that are more equitable, positive, and inclusive. Eligible coalitions and collaboratives can apply for two-year operating grants ranging from $40,000 to $150,000 . The opportunity is particularly relevant for organizations and collaborative groups that are working to use sport and play as tools for youth development and broader community change. Applications for the MOVE Fund 2026 opened on August 24, 2026 , and eligible applicants must submit their applications by September 16, 2026 . In addition to the funding opportunity, the MOVE Fund is hosting a MOVE Fund 2026 Webinar on September 2, 2026 , where prospective applicants can learn more about the fund and its priorities. MOVE Fund 2026 Opportunity Details Opportunity: MOVE Fund 2026 Category: Grant Grant Type: Two-year operating grant Grant Amount: $40,000 to $150,000 Application Opening Date: August 24, 2026 Application Deadline: September 16, 2026 Webinar Date: September 2, 2026 Webinar Time: 8:30 PM Nairobi time Application Structure: One application per coalition or collective Lead Applicant Requirement: The lead organization must have 501(c)(3) nonprofit status What Is the MOVE Fund? The MOVE Fund is focused on supporting collaborative efforts that recognize the role that sport and play can play in youth development and community transformation . Rather than focusing exclusively on individual sports organizations, the fund is intended to support coalitions and collectives working together around broader systems-level goals. These collaborations may bring together organizations, community groups, youth development organizations, advocates, and other stakeholders seeking to improve how sport and play are supported and delivered within their regions. The fund s priorities center on three major areas: Advocating for public and private investment in sport and play Building the capacity of sport-based youth development organizations Creating equitable, positive, and inclusive local sports systems This makes the opportunity potentially valuable for collaborative initiatives that want to move beyond individual programs and contribute to longer-term changes within their local or regional sports ecosystems. What Will the MOVE Fund Support? The MOVE Fund will support coalitions and collectives whose work aligns with its stated priorities. Applicants should demonstrate how their collaborative efforts contribute to strengthening sport and play as important tools for youth development and community development. 1. Advocacy for Investment in Sport and Play One of the key priorities of the MOVE Fund is supporting coalitions that advocate for increased public and private investment in sport and play . This may be particularly relevant to collaborative groups working to influence: Government investment in sports infrastructure and programming Private-sector investment in sport and youth initiatives Funding for community-based sports programs Policies that improve access to sport and play Investment in youth-focused sports development Greater recognition of sport and play as tools for positive youth development Community-level or regional strategies for strengthening sports ecosystems Coalitions involved in advocacy should be able to demonstrate how their collective efforts can contribute to stronger investment and support for sport and play. 2. Capacity Building for Sport-Based Youth Development Organizations The MOVE Fund also seeks to support work that builds the capacity of sport-based youth development organizations . Capacity building can involve strengthening the ability of organizations to design, implement, manage, evaluate, and sustain programs that use sport and play to support young people. Collaboratives working in this area may focus on strengthening organizational systems, improving leadership, developing partnerships, enhancing program quality, or building the long-term sustainability of organizations serving young people through sport. The emphasis on capacity building means that the opportunity is not necessarily limited to organizations delivering sports activities. It can also be relevant to collaborative efforts aimed at strengthening the organizations and systems behind youth sports development. 3. Building Equitable, Positive and Inclusive Local Sports Systems A third major priority is supporting coalitions that work to create local sports systems that are equitable, positive, and inclusive . This recognizes that access to sport and play can be influenced by factors such as resources, community infrastructure, organizational capacity, inclusion, and opportunities available to young people. Coalitions applying to the MOVE Fund should therefore consider how their work contributes to creating sports environments where young people and communities can participate meaningfully and benefit from positive sporting experiences. How Much Funding Is Available? Successful applicants can receive two-year operating grants ranging from $40,000 to $150,000 . The operating-grant structure is important because it indicates that the funding is intended to help support the broader work of eligible coalitions and collectives rather than being limited to a narrowly defined one-time activity. Depending on the approved grant amount and the needs of the collaborative, funding could provide important support for activities related to advocacy, capacity development, coalition coordination, systems strengthening, and other work aligned with the MOVE Fund s priorities. Applicants should carefully review the fund s official guidance and application requirements before determining the appropriate funding request. Who Can Apply for the MOVE Fund 2026? The opportunity is specifically designed for coalitions and collectives/collaboratives whose work aligns with the MOVE Fund s priorities. Importantly, the fund states that coalitions or collaboratives at various stages of development are encouraged to apply , provided that their work aligns with the fund s priorities. This means that an applicant does not necessarily have to be an established, highly developed coalition to be considered. Emerging and developing collaborative efforts may also be encouraged to apply if they can demonstrate alignment with the fund s objectives. Instead, the coalition should agree on its lead organization and coordinate the submission as a single collective application. This makes internal planning and communication particularly important.
